opus-5.5.text:
Well, the thing that really struck me about Picbreeder, and it took years for this to sink in, is that the images people evolved there have these remarkably elegant internal representations, and nobody trained them on any data at all. There was no dataset of skulls or butterflies or cars. People were just clicking on images they found interesting, and over many generations, through this open-ended, serendipitous process, these networks came to encode things in a way that's almost modular. If you look inside a Picbreeder skull, you'll find that there are individual dimensions that correspond to something like opening and closing the mouth, or the eyes winking, and the symmetry is built in at a deep level. It's like the network actually understands what a skull is, in some sense, structurally.

Now compare that to what happens when you take a conventional network and train it with stochastic gradient descent to output that exact same image. You can get it to reproduce the picture perfectly, pixel for pixel. But when you look inside, it's a mess. We call it fractured entangled representation. The output is right, but the underlying organization is spaghetti. If you perturb a weight, you don't get a meaningful variation on a skull; you get garbage.

So this is a challenge to the idea that knowledge arises primarily from fitting lots of data toward an objective. The dominant assumption is that if you scale up data and compute, good representations will emerge. But Picbreeder shows you can get the same output with a completely different quality of internal understanding, and the path you took to get there matters enormously. The Picbreeder representations were built up incrementally. Symmetry got locked in early, then other regularities were layered on top, and each step was a discovery that made sense on its own. There was no target. In fact, the people who found the skull weren't looking for a skull.

That suggests that how something is learned, the history of the search, is a big part of what the knowledge actually is. Performance on a benchmark can't see that difference. Two systems can look identical from the outside and be profoundly different on the inside, and that difference will show up later in things like creativity, generalization, and the ability to keep building on what you know. That's why I think it's a real warning sign for the purely data-driven, objective-driven picture of intelligence.

r001.rationale: It says Picbreeder produced meaningful dimensions such as mouth opening and eye winking without training on any dataset.

r002.rationale: The response discusses a skull representation, not an apple representation or separation of stem movement from body changes.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a swinging stem or interpret that behavior as a hypothesis about the world.

r004.rationale: It questions data-driven accounts of intelligence broadly, but does not ask whether human hypotheses arise from elegant internal representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing that's always struck me about Picbreeder is that nobody was trying to make the things that came out of it. There was no dataset of skulls or butterflies or cars that the system was trained on. There's no target. People just pick what they find interesting, and they branch from what somebody else found interesting, and over thousands of those little choices you get these images that look like real objects. And then when you open up the networks underneath, you find something even stranger, which is that the representation is beautifully organized. There's a single parameter that opens and closes the mouth of the skull. There's symmetry baked in because symmetry was discovered early, before anyone knew it was going to become a skull. The network has essentially decomposed the world into the right pieces, and nobody ever told it what the right pieces were.

Now contrast that with the data-driven picture, where the story is that knowledge comes from exposure. You get enough examples, you compress them, and out of the compression comes understanding. That's the dominant paradigm right now, and it clearly works for a lot of things. But Picbreeder shows you can get regularity, modularity, something that looks a lot like genuine understanding of structure, without any of that. The structure came from the search process itself, from the history of what was stumbled upon and kept, not from statistics over examples.

And I think the reason that's a challenge, and not just a curiosity, is that it suggests the way you arrive at a representation matters as much as what the representation can do. When we trained networks with SGD to reproduce those exact same Picbreeder images, they could do it. Same output, pixel for pixel. But the internal representation was a tangled mess. You couldn't find the mouth parameter. Change one weight and the whole thing falls apart. So two systems that are behaviorally identical, and one of them actually understands something about the image and the other one doesn't, and the only difference is the path they took to get there. That's a hard thing to explain if you believe knowledge is just a function of the data.

So my view is that there's a kind of knowledge that comes from open-ended exploration, from serendipity and divergence, that you can't get by throwing more examples at a system. And Picbreeder is maybe the clearest little existence proof of that that I know of.

r001.rationale: It says Picbreeder produced meaningful structure, such as a parameter controlling a skull’s mouth, without a dataset or target from the world.

r002.rationale: It discusses a skull representation, not an evolved apple representation separating stem movement from body changes.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a swinging stem or interpret that behavior as a hypothesis about the world.

r004.rationale: It argues that representation can arise through exploration rather than data, but does not ask whether human hypotheses arise from the elegance of internal representations.

astra-6.text:
Well, the interesting thing about Picbreeder is that nobody gives it a dataset of the thing it eventually discovers. You don’t feed it pictures of cars and say, “Learn what a car is.” People select images they find interesting, those images produce variations, and over many generations you might arrive at something that looks like a car. And the person who gets there may have been following something that looked entirely different just a few steps earlier.

Now, you could say that human selection supplies information, and that’s true. This isn’t knowledge appearing from nowhere. But that doesn’t fully explain the representation that evolves underneath the image. The system evolves a network that generates the image, and that network can capture regularities—symmetry, repetition, relationships between parts. When you mutate it, sometimes you get changes that seem surprisingly meaningful: a feature changes coherently instead of the whole picture just dissolving into noise.

So the challenge is to the idea that a useful representation must come from extracting patterns from examples of the thing represented. Here, the representation emerges through a historical process of discovery, without that thing being the target all along. The stepping stones matter. Something that becomes useful for representing a car might have arisen when nobody was thinking about cars at all.

That suggests that if we want to understand how knowledge arises, we have to look beyond fitting a model to a fixed collection of observations. We also have to understand the process that creates new things to observe, new possibilities to explore, and representations that make further discoveries possible.

r001.rationale: The response says Picbreeder develops coherent, meaningful features in its image-generating representation without being trained on examples of the thing represented.

r002.rationale: It does not mention an evolved apple representation or distinguish stem movement from changes to the apple’s body.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a swinging stem or interpret such behavior as an accurate hypothesis about the world.

r004.rationale: It does not ask whether human hypotheses arise from the elegance of internal representations; it discusses discovery processes more generally.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the interesting thing about Picbreeder is that nobody ever specified the final image as a target. People would select images they found interesting, branch off from other people’s discoveries, and keep going. So you might end up with something that looks like a car, but there was never a dataset of cars that the system was trying to fit.

And then you can look inside the evolved network and ask what it represents. You can find surprisingly meaningful structure: parts of the image can vary together in coherent ways. That structure emerged through a history of stepping stones, many of which didn’t look anything like the eventual result.

Now, that doesn’t mean there was no information coming in. Human selection matters, and so does the encoding. But it challenges the idea that acquiring a representation is fundamentally about absorbing examples of the thing you ultimately represent. In Picbreeder, the representation is constructed through an exploratory process. The system arrives at something that nobody knew they were looking for, with internal structure that helps make that discovery possible. So I think we need an account of where knowledge comes from that includes that kind of open-ended invention.
